definition: An associative classifier (AC) is a kind of supervised learning model that uses association rules to assign a target value.
details: The term associative classification was coined by Bing Liu et al., in which the authors defined a model made of rules "whose right-hand side are restricted to the classification class attribute".

explainer.lead: An associative classifier makes predictions with if–then rules learned from labelled examples. It adapts association rules to classification by requiring each rule to end in a class, giving predictions a readable form.

tiers.eli5: Think of rules like "if a basket has bread and butter, it also has jam". An associative classifier builds rules of that shape, but every rule ends in the class label it predicts.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers mine association rules from labelled data, keeping only rules whose right-hand side is the class attribute, then use them to predict. The pitfall sits in the rule set itself: it can grow large and requires handling to be usable for classification.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined by Bing Liu et al. as a model made of rules whose right-hand side are restricted to the classification class attribute, built via association rules to assign a target value. The definition specifies the rule form, not selection or scoring criteria.

explainer.example: Given weather records labelled with whether a match was played, a classifier might learn “if outlook = sunny and humidity = high, then play = no.” A new day matching both conditions is assigned the class “no.”
explainer.intuition: The idea is to classify by combining pattern discovery with readable rules: find conditions associated with known outcomes, then use rules pointing to a class to label new cases.
howItWorks: Start with training examples and their known target values.
Find association rules linking attribute conditions to outcomes.
Keep rules whose right-hand side is the class attribute.
Apply the resulting rule-based classifier to assign a target value.
explainer.whyItMatters: It turns association rules into a supervised classifier while expressing decisions as explicit if–then statements. The class restriction distinguishes these classification rules from associations between arbitrary attributes.
misconceptions: It is supervised learning, not classification without labelled outcomes.
Not every association rule qualifies: its right-hand side must be the class attribute.
It is a rule-based classifier, not merely a collection of unrelated patterns.
